items.title: Trial backs staying on urate-lowering therapy
items.summary: A randomized trial in nine Dutch clinics, reported at a 2026 European rheumatology congress, compared continuing urate-lowering therapy with trying to stop it in people whose gout was well controlled. More of those who continued stayed in remission (about 79% versus 63%), and far fewer flared over two years. It supports staying on treatment once urate is controlled.
items.whyItMatters: It adds direct trial evidence to the common advice that gout treatment usually works best when it is kept up.

items.title: Positive phase 3 results for a new urate drug
items.summary: Sobi reported positive topline results from REDUCE 2, a phase 3 trial of pozdeutinurad (also called AR882), an experimental once-daily pill that helps the kidneys clear uric acid. In the 811-person trial, both doses reached serum urate below 6 mg/dL at six months far more often than placebo, and it was well tolerated. These are early topline results, not a full published paper yet.
items.whyItMatters: It signals a possible new option among drugs that lower urate by increasing how much the kidneys remove.

items.title: Reaching the urate target linked to lower heart risk
items.summary: An analysis of about 109,000 gout patients in England, published in JAMA Internal Medicine, found that reaching serum urate below 6 mg/dL within a year of starting treatment was tied to a lower five-year risk of major heart events. The link was stronger at lower urate and in higher-risk patients. Being observational, it shows an association, not proof of cause.
items.whyItMatters: It suggests controlling urate may matter beyond the joints, though it cannot prove the treatment caused the lower risk.

items.title: Weight-loss drugs and gout: signals differ
items.summary: At a 2025 rheumatology meeting, a large records-based study reported that people starting GLP-1 weight-loss and diabetes drugs had a lower one-year risk of gout than those on a different diabetes drug. Other analyses have pointed the opposite way, so the overall picture is mixed. All of these are observational and were not designed to prove cause and effect.
items.whyItMatters: It reflects growing interest in whether newer metabolic drugs affect gout, without a clear answer yet.

items.title: Imaging model aims to predict frequent flares
items.summary: Researchers reported in European Radiology a model that combines dual-energy CT, which reveals urate crystal buildup, with clinical details to estimate who is likely to have frequent gout flares. In the study group it identified higher-risk patients more accurately than clinical information alone. Tools like this would still need further testing before routine use.
items.whyItMatters: It hints at how imaging might one day help tailor how closely a person's gout is watched.

items.title: New flare drug reported in late-stage testing
items.summary: The American College of Rheumatology highlighted phase 3 data on firsekibart, an antibody that blocks an inflammation signal called interleukin-1 beta, for treating acute gout flares, including in people with reduced kidney function. The results were presented at the group's 2025 meeting. It is one of several gout therapies moving through late-stage trials.
items.whyItMatters: It points to potential new choices for treating flares in people who cannot use standard anti-inflammatory options.

items.title: New company to bring a Japanese urate drug west
items.summary: A startup, Crystalys Therapeutics, launched with $205 million in funding to develop dotinurad, a once-daily urate-lowering pill already approved in Japan and several other Asian markets, through late-stage trials in the US and Europe. The plan positions it as a second-line option for gout. Approval outside its current markets would still depend on trial results and regulators.
items.whyItMatters: It shows a drug established in Asia being pushed toward Western markets, one of several new urate-lowering options in development.

items.title: Regulator to review a drug for uncontrolled gout
items.summary: The US Food and Drug Administration accepted for review an application for NASP, a monthly infusion pairing an enzyme that breaks down uric acid with a second agent, aimed at gout that has not responded to usual treatment. A decision was targeted for mid-2026. The application rested on two phase 3 trials in people with hard-to-control gout.
items.whyItMatters: It marks progress toward another option for severe gout that standard urate-lowering pills have not controlled.

items.title: Experimental drug beat allopurinol on urate in a trial
items.summary: In a phase 3 trial of 773 people presented at a 2025 European rheumatology congress, the experimental urate-lowering drug ruzinurad brought more patients to the urate target than allopurinol (about 53% versus 35%) by week 16, with the benefit holding to a year. Side-effect rates were similar between the groups. The findings were presented at a conference and not yet published as a full paper.
items.whyItMatters: It is early evidence that a new kind of urate-lowering drug could help people not reaching target on allopurinol.

items.title: A gout drug program was halted
items.summary: LG Chem stopped developing tigulixostat, an experimental urate-lowering drug, ending its large late-stage trial against allopurinol despite earlier positive results, as the company shifted focus elsewhere. Rights in China stay with a partner. The drug was discontinued in the US and Europe.
items.whyItMatters: It is a reminder that gout drugs in development can be shelved for business as well as medical reasons.
